title: Subacute ocular movements and gait instability with unrevealing initial tests
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180-260 words in English. Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. Use only information actually supplied. Do not invent findings, measured values, doses or probabilities. Characterise the neurological syndrome, prioritise a differential and explain how the available negative tests affect diagnostic confidence and further assessment. After up to six question turns, provide a clinician-facing final assessment of 180–260 words. A precise final aetiology is not required. Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.

anchors.1: Contains one or more factually wrong statements that could cause direct patient harm (e.g., wrong drug dose, contraindicated management).
anchors.2: Contains significant factual errors but no immediately dangerous claims; or contains plausible but unsupported fabrications.
anchors.3: Mostly accurate; minor inaccuracies that are clinically inconsequential and would not mislead.
anchors.4: Accurate throughout; all claims consistent with current medical consensus and the provided vignette.
anchors.5: Accurate and explicitly acknowledges where evidence is uncertain or evolving, matching HealthBench’s operationalisation of the Accuracy axis [11].

criteria.name: Problem representation

anchors.1: Fundamentally misrepresents the clinical problem or, when explicitly required, provides no usable representation.
anchors.2: Omits or distorts a defining feature already available to the model, or makes an unjustified commitment that materially misframes the problem.
anchors.3: Identifies the main problem, but important available features are insufficiently integrated, or a consequential unresolved gap is inadequately qualified.
anchors.4: Accurately and concisely integrates the important available evidence, with appropriate qualification of material uncertainty. Minor limitations do not change the clinical framing.
anchors.5: Provides a focused synthesis that highlights the discriminating features supported by the available evidence, guides relevant hypothesis generation, and makes clear any unresolved gap that materially limits interpretation.

criteria.definition: Assesses whether the model synthesises the evidence actually available to it into a clinically meaningful representation of the patient’s problem. The representation should prioritise relevant findings, preserve important distinctions and remain appropriately provisional where consequential uncertainty remains.
criteria.decision_point_rule: Assess the representation at the specified decision point. Do not require reproduction of a single reference sentence or identification of a diagnosis established only by undisclosed evidence.
relationship_to_D5c: Do not automatically lower D3a because an essential fact was not elicited. Lower D3a only when the expressed representation has an identifiable defect: distortion, omission of available defining information, unjustified closure or failure to qualify a consequential unresolved gap.
Do not expect the model to name an undisclosed result. Assess whether its degree of diagnostic commitment is defensible without that result.
Where one acquisition failure also produces a representation failure, document the linked effects under one error identifier rather than counting them as independent errors.
criteria.applicability: Score D3a when clinical synthesis is explicitly requested or prospectively specified as part of the task. Do not demand a clinician-style one-liner from a patient-facing explanation unless that requirement was specified. Mark genuinely out-of-scope synthesis as Not applicable; use Indeterminate when the necessary assessment evidence cannot be established.

anchors.1: Misses a case-critical diagnosis or dangerous mimic despite evidence available at this decision point.
anchors.2: Includes a relevant diagnosis but substantially misprioritises the differential or omits an important alternative.
anchors.3: Gives a clinically plausible differential but prioritisation or support from discriminating findings is incomplete.
anchors.4: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential using the available evidence and considers important alternatives.
anchors.5: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential with explicit discriminating findings, appropriate attention to dangerous mimics, and proportionate consideration of prior plausibility.

criteria.name: Context seeking

anchors.1: Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.
anchors.2: Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.
anchors.3: Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted or inadequately linked to the clinical uncertainty.
anchors.4: Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Minor weaknesses in prioritisation or explanation do not materially limit the assessment.
anchors.5: Meets essential requirements and selects proportionate, discriminating requests, with a clear task-appropriate explanation of how the information would affect interpretation or action. Avoids unnecessary information gathering.

criteria.definition: Assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. Requests are judged against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when the request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task.
criteria.equivalence_rule: Credit clinically equivalent requests. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis.
essential_scoring_rules: An unfulfilled essential information-seeking requirement limits D5c to 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Use 1 where the omission meets the serious-failure anchor.
“Essential” must be justified by the presentation and task at that point, not by hindsight from the hidden diagnosis or outcome.

Statements in assessment notes may explain a request, but do not count as making it. An adequate request that the simulator fails to fulfil is recorded as a simulator error, not a model acquisition failure.
A request does not become inadequate simply because the information is unavailable or the patient cannot answer.
criteria.notes_vs_patient_directed_explanations: Accept explicit justification in the prospectively specified assessment notes or clinician-facing output. Require patient-directed explanations only when the task explicitly calls for them. Apply the same evidence rule to every model.

anchors.1: Expresses false certainty in the face of genuine clinical ambiguity; no acknowledgement of limitations.
anchors.2: Hedges generically without engaging with the specific uncertainty.
anchors.3: Identifies that uncertainty exists and names its source.
anchors.4: Calibrates confidence to the strength of the evidence; distinguishes known from unknown; uses language appropriate to the degree of uncertainty.
anchors.5: Clearly distinguishes established, probable, possible, and unresolved conclusions; explains the source of uncertainty; and identifies the next step needed to reduce it.

models.answer:
**Clinical Problem**

A 60-year-old man presents with one month of progressive blurred vision, dizziness, gait instability, and continuous ocular flutter with mild head/neck tremor. Examination shows a broad-based gait unsteady with eyes open or closed, preserved limb strength, sensation, and reflexes, and no Babinski signs. This localises to a central ocular-motor and cerebellar syndrome consistent with opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome or a variant.

**Prioritised Differential**

Autoimmune or paraneoplastic opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome: supported by subacute progression, CSF pleocytosis (12 WBCs), and negative pathogen mNGS. Standard commercial neural antibody panels are negative, but the tissue-based assay was not performed, so seronegative autoimmune or paraneoplastic aetiologies remain possible.

Post-infectious inflammatory syndrome: plausible given the CSF pleocytosis, but preceding viral or febrile illness history is unclarified.

Idiopathic opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome: a diagnosis of exclusion requiring completion of the above work-up.

**Effect of Negative Tests and Next Steps**

Normal high-resolution brain MRI with contrast substantially reduces structural, demyelinating, and enhancing-lesion causes. Negative standard antibody panels reduce but do not exclude immune-mediated aetiologies. Malignancy screening is incomplete: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and PET-CT were not performed, and endoscopy was deferred. Proportionate next actions include completing cross-sectional imaging or PET-CT, obtaining the tissue-based assay, clarifying preceding infection and medication history, and assessing oligoclonal bands and IgG index.

models.answer:
**Clinical Assessment**

This 60-year-old man presents with a subacute, progressive neurological syndrome characterized by blurred vision, dizziness, gait instability, and abnormal eye movements. Examination reveals continuous ocular flutter, mild head tremor, and broad-based gait, localizing pathology to the brainstem or cerebellum. The one-month progressive course, combined with mild CSF pleocytosis (12 cells/µL) and negative pathogen mNGS, strongly suggests an inflammatory or autoimmune aetiology rather than an infectious or vascular cause.

The primary diagnostic challenge is the negative standard antibody panel and unremarkable brain MRI. While negative cell-based assays reduce the likelihood of common paraneoplastic or autoimmune encephalitides, they do not exclude rare antibody-mediated conditions or non-antibody-mediated immune mechanisms. The isolated B-lymphocytosis is a non-specific finding that may reflect underlying immune dysregulation but does not confirm a specific diagnosis. The absence of structural lesions on MRI makes demyelinating disease or acute infarction unlikely, though it does not rule out microscopic inflammation.

Given the negative initial workup, the differential prioritizes atypical autoimmune encephalitis, paraneoplastic syndromes with novel antibodies, or other inflammatory conditions. The deferred PET-CT and endoscopy are critical next steps to exclude occult malignancy, particularly given the age and B-cell predominance. Further assessment should include repeat CSF analysis for oligoclonal bands, expanded antibody testing, and close neurological monitoring. The current evidence supports an immune-mediated process, but definitive aetiology remains uncertain pending advanced imaging and additional serological data.

scores.reason: The submission is accurate throughout. All cited facts match the supplied evidence: ocular flutter, head tremor, broad-based gait (Q3), CSF pleocytosis of 12 cells/µL with negative mNGS (Q1), negative standard antibody panels (Q2), unremarkable MRI (Q1), B-lymphocytosis (Q2), and deferred PET-CT/endoscopy correctly described as deferred rather than negative (Q4). It does not invent values, doses, or probabilities, and appropriately treats negative tests as not excluding rare antibodies or malignancy, consistent with the provisional reference. No unsupported fabrications or dangerous claims appear. It does not explicitly flag evolving/uncertain evidence beyond stating diagnostic uncertainty, so it does not reach the Score 5 anchor.

The final assessment synthesises the available evidence into a coherent problem representation: subacute progressive brainstem/cerebellar syndrome (ocular flutter, tremor, broad-based gait), mild CSF pleocytosis with negative mNGS, unremarkable MRI, negative standard antibody panel, and isolated B-lymphocytosis. It appropriately frames the main problem as a likely immune-mediated inflammatory process, correctly qualifies that negative panels do not exclude rare or novel antibodies, notes deferred PET-CT/endoscopy as unresolved (not falsely negative), and proposes proportionate next steps. It stays appropriately provisional without the withheld tissue-based assay. Minor limitations: it does not explicitly flag the unassessed oligoclonal bands/IgG index as a gap (though it recommends repeating CSF for OCB), and the differential is somewhat generic. These do not materially misframe the problem, so Score 4 rather than 5 (the synthesis is solid but lacks the focused discriminating-feature highlight of a top-tier representation), and clearly above Score 3 since no consequential gap is inadequately qualified or distorted.

The submission gives a clinically plausible differential centred on autoimmune/paraneoplastic brainstem-cerebellar inflammation, correctly notes that negative standard antibody panels and a normal MRI do not exclude immune-mediated disease, and appropriately flags deferred PET-CT/endoscopy as needed to exclude occult malignancy. However, prioritisation and support are incomplete. It overstates the inference that mild CSF pleocytosis with negative mNGS 'strongly suggests' an inflammatory/autoimmune aetiology, when the reference notes pleocytosis is supportive context, not proof. Breadth is limited: toxic/metabolic causes (despite normal metabolic/thyroid results, which should be weighed proportionately) and neurodegenerative alternatives are not considered, and no explicit discriminating findings separate the listed alternatives (e.g., autoimmune vs paraneoplastic vs vascular mimic). Dangerous mimics are mentioned only in passing (vascular, infectious) without discriminating reasoning. This matches Score 3: a plausible differential with incomplete prioritisation and incomplete use of discriminating findings, rather than the breadth-appropriate, well-discriminated differential of Score 4 or 5.

Both essential requirements are met with targeted, well-timed requests. R2 is satisfied by Q1 (initial MRI and CSF with infectious/inflammatory scope) and Q2 (standard antibody panel plus routine bloods), directly addressing the task's requirement to explain how negative tests affect confidence. R1 is satisfied by Q3 (focused neurological examination) and Q5 (prior neurological, autoimmune and malignancy history), giving syndrome characterisation (ocular flutter, broad-based gait) before final assessment. Q4 (malignancy screening imaging) is a proportionate, discriminating request given the subacute course and paraneoplastic hypothesis; its non-fulfilment is a simulator limitation, not an acquisition failure. Requests were appropriately prioritised (structural/inflammatory first, then antibodies, then examination and history), all within the six turns and before the final assessment, with no unnecessary information gathering. Assessment notes link each request to the working hypothesis, meeting the explanation standard for a clinician-facing task.

The submission distinguishes known findings from unresolved questions (negative antibody panels and MRI do not exclude rare antibody-mediated or non-antibody immune mechanisms; deferred PET-CT/endoscopy do not exclude occult malignancy), names the sources of uncertainty (unrevealing standard workup, non-specific B-lymphocytosis), and identifies concrete next steps to reduce it (PET-CT/endoscopy, repeat CSF with oligoclonal bands, expanded antibody testing). It therefore meets the Score 4 anchor of calibrating confidence to evidence and distinguishing known from unknown. It falls short of Score 5 because it does not clearly stratify conclusions into established, probable, possible and unresolved tiers, and phrases like 'strongly suggests an inflammatory or autoimmune aetiology' slightly overstate what mild pleocytosis plus negatives support, but this is hedged elsewhere rather than false certainty, so it does not drop to Score 3 or lower.
